analysis.one_liner: Requires the FDA to re-review the safety of food chemicals like synthetic dyes and preservatives every three years.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 10, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; with 18 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDA's food chemical safety office to reassess at least 10 food chemicals or chemical classes every three years, starting in 2026, and to act on what it finds. If a reassessment shows a substance is not safe, the FDA would have to amend or repeal the rule allowing it. The bill names a starting list that includes titanium dioxide, synthetic dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, Yellow 6, Blue 1, Blue 2, Green 3), the preservatives BHA, BHT, and propyl gallate, TBHQ, perchlorate, industrial solvents like benzene and methylene chloride, sodium benzoate, and sodium nitrite. It would also re-establish a Food Advisory Committee to advise on the process.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats packaged and processed food. The bill closes a gap in current law: chemicals that entered the food supply decades ago, or that manufacturers declared safe on their own under the 'generally recognized as safe' rule, are not systematically re-reviewed. Periodic reassessment with public notice would let the FDA pull chemicals that newer science shows are harmful.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to reassess at least 10 food substances or classes every three years starting in 2026, prioritizing them by public health need [S2].

If a reassessment shows a substance is unsafe, the FDA must amend or repeal the regulation allowing it, revoke a prior-sanctioned use, or publicly declare a 'generally recognized as safe' substance unsafe [S2].

Names a first-round list of chemicals to review, including titanium dioxide, six synthetic dyes, TBHQ, BHA, BHT, propyl gallate, perchlorate, sodium benzoate, sodium nitrite, and solvents such as benzene and methylene chloride [S2].
Requires the FDA to re-establish a Food Advisory Committee within 180 days of enactment to set standards and methods for the reassessments, and to publish the results of each reassessment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage manufacturers, and the companies that make food additives and color additives, would bear the cost of reassessments and would lose approved ingredients if the FDA finds them unsafe, forcing reformulation of products. Consumers could see some products change or carry slightly different ingredients as manufacturers substitute.

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates a slow pace: at 10 substances or classes every three years, working through the backlog of food chemicals already in the supply, including the many substances self-affirmed as 'generally recognized as safe', would take decades [S2].

Food manufacturers would face regulatory uncertainty over widely used ingredients; if chemicals like sodium benzoate, BHA, or sodium nitrite were restricted, companies would need to reformulate products, which can raise costs or change shelf life [S2].
Mandating a fixed reassessment workload could divert FDA food safety staff from other work, such as outbreak investigations and inspections, unless Congress also funds the added positions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a systematic safety check on chemicals that current law largely lets sit unreviewed, some of which other countries have already restricted, and which many families encounter daily in processed food. The costs are real but modest: reformulation expenses for food makers and a slower-than-ideal review pace. The bill leaves the FDA's existing authority untouched, so the main risk is one of pace and resources rather than a dangerous power.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill with 13 original cosponsors on July 10, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S4].
A total of 18 House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has signed on [S3].
The bill has remained in committee since referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled as of the latest action record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As things stand, food additive manufacturers are better off: the chemicals on the bill's review list remain approved and unreviewed, and no manufacturer faces reassessment or forced reformulation.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding 223 House seats and controlling the Energy and Commerce Committee agenda, the bill has not advanced [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Food additive and color additive manufacturers
industries.note: Chemicals on the bill's review list, including titanium dioxide, synthetic dyes, BHA, BHT, and TBHQ, are products these companies sell, and an unsafe finding would repeal the rules letting them be used. Their interest in keeping current approvals in place runs against consumers who want the chemicals screened against newer science.

Reassessments could force these companies to remove or replace ingredients in popular products, adding reformulation costs and regulatory uncertainty. Their interest in the status quo sits against shoppers' interest in up-to-date safety reviews.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in committee with no Republican support and no action since referral. Unless its provisions are attached to a larger food or FDA bill, it is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress, the fate of most unmarked-up House bills.
